## Per-chapter highlights

### Chapter 1 — ‘Be Strong and of a Good Courage’: The LORD Commissions Joshua

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, inheritance

After Moses' death, the LORD speaks directly to Joshua and gives the foundational charge for entering the land. The five-fold "be strong and of a good courage" formula completes its installation across Deut 31 and Joshua 1, spoken by Moses, by the LORD, and finally by the people themselves to Joshua. The chapter is the narrative-prophetic culmination of the Joshua- succession typological framework that Num 27 first installed.

### Chapter 2 — Rahab and the Spies: ‘The LORD Your God, He Is God in Heaven Above’

*status:* draft
*themes:* prophetic-call, covenant, holiness

Joshua sends two spies to Jericho; they lodge with Rahab the harlot, who hides them under flax-stalks on her rooftop. Rahab's confession at 2:9-11 — "the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath" — installs the chapter's theological center: a Canaanite woman declaring full monotheistic recognition of YHWH. The chapter has substantial NT reception: Hebrews 11:31 (faith-paradigm), James 2:25 (faith-and-works), and Matthew 1:5 (messianic genealogy inclusion).

### Chapter 3 — Crossing the Jordan: The Ark, the Priests, and the Waters Stood Up at Adam

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

Israel breaks camp at Shittim and comes to the Jordan; the priests bearing the ark of the covenant lead the people, and when their feet touch the river's brim the waters cut off and stand up in a heap at the city Adam upstream. The new generation crosses on dry ground — narratively echoing the first generation's Red Sea crossing under Moses, with the chapter opening the two-chapter Joshua 3-4 unit whose memorial-stones framework follows.

### Chapter 4 — The Twelve Stones: ‘When Your Children Shall Ask in Time to Come’

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, inheritance, prophetic-call

The Jordan-crossing's structural-completion. Twelve men, one from each tribe, take twelve stones from the riverbed and pitch them at Gilgal as a perpetual memorial; Joshua sets up a parallel twelve stones in the riverbed where the priests stood. The chapter installs the intergenerational-memory pedagogy framework ("when your children shall ask"), explicitly paralleling the Jordan crossing to the Red Sea crossing, and registers the LORD's magnification of Joshua before all Israel.

### Chapter 5 — Gilgal Circumcision, Passover, and the Captain of the LORD's Host

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, holiness, prophetic-call

The new generation enters the land as a covenant-marked people: the Gilgal circumcision rolls away the reproach of Egypt, the Passover at Gilgal closes the manna era, and Joshua encounters the captain of the LORD's host outside Jericho with a drawn sword and the same holy-ground command Moses received at the burning bush. The chapter installs three theologically-substantive units in immediate succession.

### Chapter 6 — The Fall of Jericho: ‘By Faith the Walls of Jericho Fell Down’

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, holiness

The seven-day march around Jericho — six days of one circuit, and on the seventh day seven circuits with the priests blowing the trumpets and the people shouting — culminates in the walls falling down flat and the herem framework's execution, with Rahab and her household alone preserved per the Josh 2 oath. Hebrews 11:30 reads the chapter as the conquest's faith-paradigm, paired with Heb 11:31's reading of Rahab.

### Chapter 7 — Achan and the Defeat at Ai: ‘Israel Hath Sinned’

*status:* draft
*themes:* covenant, holiness, prophetic-call

Achan violates the herem at Jericho, Israel is defeated at Ai, and the LORD declares ‘Israel hath sinned’ — singular, collective-juridical. Achan is identified by lot through tribe, family, and household; he confesses; he is stoned and burned in the Valley of Achor, where the framework Hosea 2:15 will later read as the door-of-hope. The chapter is the OT's hardest single installation of the covenantal-collective-responsibility framework.

### Chapter 8 — Ai Retaken + the Gerizim/Ebal Covenant Ceremony Executed

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, holiness

Israel returns to Ai with the LORD's ambush instructions and takes the city; the king is hanged on a tree until eventide and taken down before sundown per the Deut 21:22-23 framework. Joshua then leads the people to Mount Ebal, builds the altar of unhewn stones, inscribes the law, and executes the Gerizim/Ebal antiphonal blessing-and-curse ceremony Moses had commanded — framework's cross-session completion across four sessions of the project's drafting work.

### Chapter 9 — The Gibeonite Deception and the Oath That Held

*status:* published
*themes:* covenant, prophetic-call, holiness

The Gibeonites disguise themselves as travelers from a far country with moldy bread and worn garments; Israel's leaders swear a peace-covenant without consulting the LORD. Three days later the deception is discovered, but the oath binds Israel — the Gibeonites become hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and the altar. The covenant's juridical force is later tested at 2 Samuel 21:1-9 when Saul's violation triggers a three-year famine in David's reign.
